newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman prepares free-market agenda for Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Aleman prepares free-market agenda for Nicaragua.

text.p: With his presidential election win almost in the bag, right-winger Arnoldo Aleman must now focus on the monumental task of rebuilding Nicaragua's economy, one of the poorest in Latin America, analysts said on Saturday.

After Aleman's apparent win over former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega in Sunday's vote, jubilant businessmen rushed to congratulate the burly former Managua mayor, trading soared on Nicaragua's tiny stock market and prominent bankers danced at Aleman's Liberal Alliance headquarters.

While election authorities are still reviewing the vote count, Aleman's still-unofficial victory seemed assured as analysts doubted any discrepencies found could overcome his 49 to 38 percent lead over Ortega.

The opposition has protested "serious irregularities" in the vote count, but Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council on Friday said the election would not be annulled and international observers have discounted allegations of fraud.

But the business community's joy that Ortega, who headed Nicaragua's 1979-1990 Marxist government, will not come back to power may be short-lived as the reality of Nicaragua's deep economic problems sinks in.
"This is a desperately poor, indebted economy kept artificially alive on an artificial respirator of foreign aid," Nicaraguan economist Mario Arana told Reuters.

Nicaragua, once known as the "bread basket" of Central America for its abundant farmland, became the region's economic basket case in the late 1980s, when it was devastated by an eight-year war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels and economic mismanagement by the Marxist Sandinista government.

In the 1990s President Violeta Chamorro rolled back many of the Sandinista's economic changes, introducing a tough, free-market austerity programme that controlled inflation and brought economic growth but did little to create jobs or reduce poverty.
The World Bank has projected growth in 1996 to be 4.6 percent and inflation to hover at 11.5 percent.

Aleman has promised to make Nicaragua Central America's bread basket once again through a free-market economic policy that prioritizes agriculture, the backbone of the Nicaraguan economy, and attracting foreign investment.

His vice-presidential candidate Enrique Bolanos said the government would create 100,000 jobs in its first year "if the opposition is rational", a reference to the Sandinistas who won a solid bloc of seats in the National Assembly.
But his challenge will be enormous in this country, which a 1996 U.N. study rated as the least-developed country in the Americas after Haiti.

The statistics are devastating. More than half the work-age population lacks a decent job, 75 percent of the population has unsatisfied basic needs, per capita annual income is $454 and clusters of hungry children begging for change crowd intersections.

And for those Nicaraguans who have jobs, the wages are miserable. A doctor in a state hospital earns about $100 a month, while nurses earn $50-60 a month. The buying power of salaries has fallen by 60 percent since 1990, economists said.

Nicaragua carries one of the heaviest debt burdens in relation to the size of its economy, totalling more than $10 billion, five times its entire gross domestic product, according to Central Bank figures.
Aleman has said he will continue the general outlines of Chamorro's macroeconomic programme, including the structural adjustment programme she negotiated with the International Monetary Fund.
But he said he will follow a more populist policy than Chamorro, favouring small- and mid-sized farmers rather than Nicaragua's powerful oligarchy favoured by Chamorro.
